why: The classic rotated search: at every mid, at least one half [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is sorted, and checking whether the target lies inside that sorted half tells you which half to keep.
hints: A rotated array is not sorted, but cut it anywhere and one of the two pieces is.

If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: keep it if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], else go right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: keep it if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], else go left.
Standard lo <= hi loop returning mid on a hit, -1 at the end. O(log n). (Alternative: find the minimum's index first, then binary search the right run.)
pitfalls: Use <= in nums[lo] <= nums[mid]: when lo == mid the left half is one element and is sorted.
The range test must be strict on the side of mid (target < nums[mid]) since nums[mid] was already checked.
constraints:
• 1 <= nums.length <= 105
  • -109 <= nums[i], target <= 109
  • All values are distinct.
  • nums is a strictly increasing array rotated at an unknown pivot (possibly not rotated at all).
  • Aim for O(log n) time.
